entries.text: R-20261104-BINANCE-POSTHACK-OUTFLOWS new catch-up RISKS_CRYPTO_LIQUIDITY Binance customers have withdrawn a net US$4.72bn after exchange reopening Reuters' newly published crypto roundup reported net customer withdrawals of US$4.72 billion after Binance reopened following last week's hack. entries.text: credit-2026-11-02 credit Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive · post-week review 2026-11-02 Research verified 2 Nov · week ended 30 Oct; not Friday 08:00 knowledge Verified extract The new post-week review verifies Microsoft final pricing, adds P&G issuance terms and examines BIS cross-border credit and Bank of England non-bank research. Prior Friday editions remain archived. Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive · post-week review Week ended 30 October 2026 · research verified 2 November This newly completed scheduled edition includes final issuance documents and the completed week. It is not a reconstruction of information available at 08:00 Singapore time on Friday. This public extract retains only independently checked material; the earlier 30 October edition is unchanged. 1. Microsoft: final pricing replaces preliminary borrowing context Microsoft's SEC pricing sheet is dated 29 October, with expected settlement on 4 November. Eight fixed-rate tranches total US$23bn; two floating-rate tranches of US$1bn each bring the offering to US$25bn. The following are issue terms, not current market quotes. Maturity · USD principal · coupon · issue price per 100 · issuance YTM · stated benchmark spread 2036 · $4bn · 5.550% · 99.659 · 5.595% · +65bp 2046 · $2bn · 6.150% · 99.624 · 6.183% · +85bp 2056 · $4bn · 6.250% · 99.919 · 6.256% · +95bp 2066 · $2bn · 6.350% · 99.914 · 6.356% · +105bp The 2066 note is benchmarked to the Treasury due May 2056, not a 40-year Treasury. The floating-rate notes use compounded SOFR plus a margin; no fixed YTM is inferred for them. 2. Non-AI corporate issuance P&G's 26 October SEC document specifies four USD tranches totalling US$4bn. Its 2056 tranche has a 5.900% coupon, 99.860 issue price, 5.910% issue YTM and +60bp over its stated Treasury benchmark. Four verified P&G tranches are added to the existing 26–27 October monitor; Microsoft is detailed separately above because it priced on 29 October. 3. Cross-border credit is a dated stock, not delinquency BIS statistics released 29 October place cross-border bank credit at US$40.7tn at end-June 2026, with 11% annual growth. The Q2 increase was US$877bn: US$560bn in loans/deposits and US$317bn in bank-held debt securities. These global banking aggregates are not U.S. household arrears or current November credit losses. 4. Non-bank transmission and AI financing The Bank of England's 23 October Working Paper 1212 models banks and non-bank intermediaries using UK data. Conventional rate-policy transmission changes little with non-bank size in the model, while QE transmission depends on how that sector expands. This is model-based research, not an observed default forecast. The BIS AI-financing bulletin connects long-term borrowing, off-balance-sheet structures and institutional funding. Its event-study findings do not establish a persistent Treasury-yield increase caused by AI issuance. 5. Analysis and coverage limits Separate duration risk, issuer credit risk and funding risk. Review legal borrower, collateral priority, liquidity and cash interest coverage. A downgrade, late payment, nonaccrual and realised investor loss are different events. Existing household-credit metrics retain their Q2 2026 label. New rating-action ratios, private-credit default estimates and unverified financing terms were omitted from this extract; no personal account amounts or borrowing balances are included. Official Friday Treasury yields and ECB reference crosses accompany the election update. U.S. Election Daily Brief · 1 November 2026 Singapore morning edition · U.S. reporting through Saturday, 31 October Verified extract of the newest completed three-part scheduled briefing. Source snapshots and units are retained below. Open the original chat for the complete styled report. Unverified legal-news details, individual surveys, approval figures, prediction-market prices and calendar entries are omitted. 1. National polling RealClearPolling's generic congressional ballot average shows Democrats at 51.5% and Republicans at 43.1%, a Democratic lead of 8.4 percentage points. Included survey fieldwork spans 8–29 October. These vote-intention averages are not probabilities of chamber control. The lead is 0.2 percentage points wider than the prior archived edition; this alone does not establish a statistically significant overnight swing. 2. House and Senate forecasts Decision Desk HQ's 31 October 5:26 PM U.S. Eastern snapshot gives Democrats an 83% probability of House control with 241 projected seats, and a 63% probability of Senate control with 52 projected seats. Both probabilities are one percentage point above the prior archived snapshot. Forecast probabilities and seat projections are not election results. Close races and correlated polling errors remain central to Senate uncertainty. 3. Last completed Treasury session · Friday, 30 October Official U.S. Treasury par yields were 4.94% for 10 years and 5.31% for 30 years, down four and one basis points from 29 October. The dashboard reference curve is now dated 30 October: 1Y 4.36%, 2Y 4.56%, 3Y 4.65%, 5Y 4.71%, 7Y 4.80%, 10Y 4.94%, 20Y 5.34%, 30Y 5.31%. These are constant-maturity par yields, not a specific bond's coupon, purchase yield, issuance yield or executable price. There is no new weekend Treasury close. 4. FX reference snapshot · Friday, 30 October ECB reference rates per EUR were USD 1.1172, SGD 1.4282 and CHF 0.9194. Dividing the non-USD rates by the USD rate gives USD/SGD 1.2784 and USD/CHF 0.8230, rounded to four decimals. These calculated reference crosses are informational, not live bank quotes or New York closing prices. 5. Conditional market implications The briefing considers greater fiscal and regulatory confrontation under a Democratic sweep, budget bargaining under divided government, and deficit, inflation and issuance risks under Republican control. These are research scenarios, not observed returns or bond-price forecasts. Earnings and AI capital-spending concerns are separate market catalysts; no election outcome is inferred from the last trading session. Assess duration and funding currency together. Falling yields can support existing fixed-rate bonds, while currency movements can offset that benefit in a cross-currency-funded position. No personal positions, borrowing balances or allocations are published. 6. Publication record The 30 October source-unavailable election record and 31 October verified extract remain unchanged. The new earnings edition is dated 1 November with an explicit 08:00 SGT cutoff. Four active and eleven paused task titles and states were rechecked; no schedules were changed. The latest Friday credit edition remains 30 October. entries.text: election-2026-10-31 election U.S. Election Daily Brief 2026-10-31 08:14 SGT delivery · 30 Oct source snapshots DDHQ favours Democrats for both chambers; national polling is unchanged. Verified election, equity-close and FX observations from the completed morning briefing. Verified extract U.S. Election Daily Brief · 31 October 2026 Verified extract of the completed 08:14 SGT scheduled briefing. Selected claims were checked against their underlying sources before publication. This is an edited research summary; open the original styled chat for the complete briefing. Unverified benchmark Treasury quotations, prediction-market prices, approval figures and some news details have been omitted. 1. National polling RealClearPolling's generic congressional ballot average was Democrats 51.4%, Republicans 43.2%, a Democratic lead of 8.2 percentage points. The included survey window was 8–26 October. The briefing describes the average as unchanged from 30 October. Poll publication dates and survey fieldwork dates are different; this does not establish a new overnight swing. 2. House and Senate forecasts Decision Desk HQ, updated 30 October at 2:39 PM U.S. Eastern, assigned Democrats an 82% probability of House control, projecting 239 seats. Its Senate probability was 62%, with 52 projected Democratic seats. These are model forecasts, not vote shares or election results. The closest Senate forecasts in the source were Kansas 53%, Iowa 55%, Ohio 55%, Alaska 60%, Maine 60%, Texas 60% and Michigan 73% Democratic win probability. DDHQ's closest House races included Iowa-02, Texas-15, Ohio-07, Florida-22, Maine-02 and Texas-35. Model uncertainty remains substantial. 3. Senate survey watch Individual polls released 30 October and listed by RCP: Kansas—Washington Post, Hamilton 54 / Marshall 44; Emerson, Hamilton 50 / Marshall 47. Texas—Quantus, Talarico 48 / Paxton 49. Alaska—Alaska Survey Research, Peltola 51 / Sullivan 49. Michigan—Rasmussen, El-Sayed 49 / Rogers 44. Earlier releases: Maine—CNN, Jackson 49 / Collins 45 on 29 October; Ohio—Suffolk, Brown 47 / Husted 44 on 28 October; Iowa—co/efficient, Turek 46 / Hinson 48 on 29 October. These are individual surveys with different methods and samples. Their margins are not probabilities and differences across pollsters are not daily changes. 4. Legal developments Reuters reported on 30 October that the Justice Department sought to prevent certification after a narrow Republican loss in Alaska, based on disputed allegations about a similarly named candidate. State officials challenged the lawsuit, and Peltola's campaign had denied involvement. These are allegations and legal proceedings, not findings of election fraud. The briefing highlights certification uncertainty as a risk to the timing of a clear Senate outcome. 5. Completed U.S. equity session At the 30 October U.S. close, the S&P 500 ended at 7,580.07, down 1.82%, and the Nasdaq Composite at 25,437.00, down 2.86%. Intel fell 28.6%. These values were checked against Reuters' closing-market report carried by AOL, updated 20:23 UTC. Reuters linked the sell-off to disappointing Intel and Amazon results and concerns about AI spending. These are session-close observations, not Saturday live quotes. 6. FX reference snapshot The ECB's 30 October EUR reference rates were USD 1.1172, SGD 1.4282 and CHF 0.9194 per EUR. Dividing each non-USD rate by the USD rate gives USD/SGD 1.2784 and USD/CHF 0.8230, rounded to four decimals. These are calculated reference crosses, not New York closing prices or executable bank rates. 7. Conditional market implications The briefing separates election scenarios from an automatic directional trade. A Democratic sweep may increase fiscal confrontation; divided control may constrain legislation while leaving budget negotiations unresolved; Republican control leaves fiscal, inflation and issuance risks to assess. These are conditional interpretations, not observed returns or forecasts of bond prices. Monitor duration, funding currency and collateral together. Falling Treasury yields may support existing bonds, while CHF appreciation can increase the USD value of CHF liabilities. A favourable move in one variable does not remove the other risks. No client positions, borrowing amounts or allocations are included. 8. Publication checks and limits The 30 October election source-unavailable record remains in edition history. The latest Friday credit edition remains 30 October, with the next original weekly delivery listed for 6 November. The 31 October earnings response is shown as delivered at 08:02 SGT but currently fails to load; its text has not been reconstructed and the 30 October verified earnings cards remain in place. Three active and ten paused tasks were rechecked; no schedules were changed. The offering size was not final. The borrowing illustrates how even highly cash-generative AI companies are increasingly considering external capital to finance infrastructure while preserving flexibility. reuters.com Rates / duration: Larger long-maturity corporate issuance creates more duration supply. Its effect on Treasury yields or credit spreads cannot be inferred from the deal size alone. Credit quality: Microsoft's strong cash flow contrasts with Amazon's trailing cash burn and Intel's near-term cash-flow warning. Debt capacity should be assessed through operating cash generation, capex obligations and refinancing costs. Inflation and supply costs: Reuters linked elevated energy prices to pressure on household expenditure and transportation margins, while higher refining and LNG margins supported energy producers. reuters.com +2 Singapore portfolio translation: For a USD bond portfolio financed in CHF or SGD, separate three risks: underlying issuer credit quality, long-duration price sensitivity and funding-currency exposure. Strong AI revenue does not automatically protect all three. 9. Action: Compare free cash flow after capex, leverage and debt costs across sectors rather than treating all earnings growth as equally valuable. entries.title: Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive
entries.text: credit-2026-10-30 credit Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive 2026-10-30 08:09 SGT delivery Duration, AI borrowing, new issuance and the path from late payment to default. Friday Bond, Credit & Debt Markets ────•❉᯽❉•──── 30 October 2026 · 8:00 AM SGT Weekly research Research cutoff: 29 October 2026, U.S. market close, subject to source publication availability. Primary focus: 23–29 October. Earlier studies are explicitly labelled as background. Executive market dashboard 10Y U.S. Treasury 4.98% 29 Oct · −2bp vs 23 Oct 30Y U.S. Treasury 5.32% 29 Oct · −1bp vs 23 Oct U.S. IG credit OAS 86bp 5bp tighter vs 23 Oct U.S. HY credit OAS 314bp 24bp tighter vs 23 Oct Treasury par yields as of 29 Oct; ICE BofA credit-index spreads as of 28 Oct, the latest published observations verified. Sources: U.S. Treasury and FRED. U.S. Department of the Treasury +2 The central development this week is the growing scale and complexity of AI debt financing, not a broad collapse in credit markets. Microsoft moved toward a reported US$25 billion bond transaction, banks and Blackstone arranged US$63 billion of AI-equipment financing for Anthropic-related infrastructure, and new BIS research documented how AI borrowing can affect insurers, private-credit funds and potentially Treasury term premiums. Meanwhile, the broad high-yield index spread actually tightened during the week. Investment interpretation: Credit stress is becoming more issuer-specific and structure-specific, while the public market remains receptive to stronger borrowers. That divergence matters. A credit index can improve while an individual leveraged AI borrower suffers a severe financing shock. 1. U.S. Treasury duration and credit spreads Latest verified yield curve Maturity 23 Oct 29 Oct Change 2Y 4.68% 4.61% −7bp 5Y 4.84% 4.78% −6bp 7Y 4.91% 4.87% −4bp 10Y 5.00% 4.98% −2bp 20Y 5.36% 5.35% −1bp 30Y 5.33% 5.32% −1bp Official U.S. Treasury par yield curve. U.S. Department of the Treasury The curve remains relatively steep from 2Y to 30Y, but the far end offers little additional yield over the 20Y point. On 29 October, the 30Y yielded 3bp less than the 20Y. For a long-duration investor, the extra ten years of maturity must therefore be justified by the bond's valuation, convexity and expected yield path, not by assuming that longer maturity necessarily pays more. Credit spreads: the index is not confirming systemic panic U.S. high-yield credit spreads ICE BofA U.S. High Yield Index OAS, basis points. Latest available observation: 28 October 2026. 310bp 320bp 330bp 340bp 350bp 22 Oct 23 Oct 26 Oct 27 Oct 28 Oct 22 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 340bp 23 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 338bp 26 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 330bp 27 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 318bp 28 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 314bp Source: FRED high-yield OAS. St. Louis Fed Index 23 Oct 28 Oct Weekly move IG corporate OAS 91bp 86bp −5bp HY corporate OAS 338bp 314bp −24bp HY less IG OAS 247bp 228bp −19bp The difference between the indexes is a simple comparison, not a duration-adjusted relative-value measure. Positioning implication: Broad HY spread tightening suggests risk appetite remained resilient through the week. That is not an invitation to buy every issuer offering a double-digit yield. The more important question is whether default probabilities, collateral coverage and refinancing prospects are diverging faster than index averages reveal. 2. Institutional research deep dive Four substantive studies and data releases were selected, including two from 23–29 October and two earlier October papers retained for their importance. A fifth Fitch credit review is included with its publication-date limitation. Research 1. BIS: Building AI on Credit Building AI on credit: structures and spillovers BIS Bulletin No. 140 · 27 October 2026 · 8-page full PDF Mathias Drehmann and Egemen Eren This is the week's most directly relevant central-bank research. BIS finding Figure Projected 2026 capex by five major U.S. hyperscalers Over US$800bn Gross bond issuance by those five firms through September US$222bn AI-linked off-balance-sheet bonds/ABS reportedly placed during 2026 US$75–100bn Estimated data-centre lease commitments, mid-2026 US$1.2tn Portion related to leases not yet commenced US$820bn These figures represent different financing categories and should not be added together as though they were all outstanding bonds. bis.org How AI borrowing risk can travel through the financial system AI hyperscalers and technology customers Lease commitments · capacity contracts · limited guarantees Data-centre and equipment SPVs Buildings · power infrastructure · GPUs · contracted revenue Banks Senior loans and construction finance Non-bank investors Private credit · insurers · ABS Simplified structure based on BIS Graph 2, not a representation of any one transaction. The BIS analysed 18 AI-financing news days during 2026. It found an estimated 1.5bp increase in the 10-year Treasury term premium on those days, generally fading within two trading days. This is an event-study association, not a demonstrated causal or persistent effect. The paper's Graph 3 and online annex explain the methodology and limitations. bis.org Why it matters: Long-dated AI corporate debt competes for some of the same institutional capital that buys Treasuries and other long-duration bonds. The immediate measured effect is small. Persistent issuance on this scale could still influence how much compensation investors demand for holding duration. Client talking point: AI investment is now large enough to matter to bond markets, even for investors who own no AI shares. Research 2. S&P: North American data-centre debt dashboard S&P Global Ratings launches interactive North America data center dashboard 23 October 2026 · Official research release and rated-transaction dataset S&P's newly published dashboard covers its rated North American data-centre transactions. 32 Rated transactions $105.3bn Total debt issuance 8.7 GW Tenant capacity Debt issuance across S&P's rated universe Corporate finance Project finance Structured-finance ABS Project finance: 58.3% Structured-finance ABS: 26.4% Corporate finance: 15.3% S&P reports 143 supporting properties and warns that power access, permitting and development constraints may affect project delivery. These figures cover S&P-rated transactions, not the entire data-centre financing market. Oct 23, 2026 Implication: The largest part of the measured debt is project finance, where the exact lender claim, sponsor support and project cash flow deserve scrutiny. The important due-diligence distinction is between a bond issued directly by a profitable hyperscaler and a security issued by a separate data-centre company that happens to have that hyperscaler as a tenant. Research 3. BIS: Bank regulation and private-credit growth Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit BIS Working Paper No. 1388 · October 2026, released 20 October · 48-page PDF · Prior-week research Authors: Sebastian Doerr, Gaston Gelos and Vesa Pursiainen. The researchers examined how U.S. bank liquidity regulation changed the provision of credit. Their central finding: A one-standard-deviation higher historical exposure to banks affected by liquidity requirements was associated with nearly 50% greater private-credit lending volume after the regulatory changes, relative to the comparison counties. bis.org This is a historical empirical estimate, not a claim that private credit grew by 50% in 2026. Credit implication: Lending risk did not simply disappear when banks became subject to tougher liquidity requirements. Some financing shifted toward non-bank vehicles. For portfolio analysis, that means reviewing the entire credit intermediation chain, especially when banks also provide leverage to the funds that ultimately hold the loans. Client talking point: Better-regulated banks do not necessarily mean every form of borrowing has become safer. Risk can migrate to institutions with different funding and transparency requirements. Research 4. Fitch: Business development company credit quality Fitch Ratings Completes Peer Review of 8 US BDCs Fitch original page dated 15 October · Research findings redistributed 28 October · Full Fitch access restricted The accessible Fitch-distributed summary states that seven BDC issuer ratings were affirmed, while New Mountain Finance's outlook moved from Stable to Negative. Indicator Finding Average realised loss rate, Fitch-rated BDCs, full-year 2025 1.1% Same group, first half 2026 0.5% First-half 2026 loss rate for the reviewed peer group 0.4% The periods are not the same length. The 0.5% first-half figure should not be compared mechanically with the 1.1% full-year figure as proof that losses have halved. Fitch expects continuing asset-quality pressure and identifies nonaccrual loans as a risk. The Lead Implication: Public BDC filings may reveal stress earlier than headline aggregate private-credit default statistics, but realised losses, nonaccruals, fair-value marks and interest coverage must be considered together. Research 5. Bank of England: Who buys long-duration corporate bonds? Domestic and foreign insurer corporate bond demand and monetary policy Staff Working Paper No. 1,210 · 9 October 2026 · 59-page PDF · Background research The study uses security-level insurer transactions from 2018–2022. It finds that UK and U.S. life insurers can respond very differently to changes in bond yields. For example, in the researchers' historical estimates, a 1 percentage-point rise in the UK 10-year government-bond yield was associated with higher net buying by UK insurers but reduced demand from U.S. insurers for their relevant UK-corporate-bond holdings over subsequent months. bankofengland.co.uk Implication: Long-duration debt demand is segmented by currency, regulatory treatment and liabilities. A 30-year bond may not have the same natural buyer base as a five-year bond. Methodological limit: Historical UK/US insurer evidence is not a forecast of October 2026 U.S. Treasury yields. 3. Latest Reuters debt and borrowing developments Microsoft: reported US$25bn bond offering Reuters · 29 October 2026 Reuters reported a planned sale of approximately US$25bn, with more than US$100bn in orders and up to ten tranches spanning roughly 2–40 years. Its SEC preliminary prospectus confirms the offering structure but leaves final pricing terms blank. Reuters +1 Classification: Announced/marketed offering. Exact coupon and final issuance yield not verified from the reviewed primary filing. Anthropic/Broadcom: US$63bn structured equipment financing Reuters · 26 October, updated 27 October 2026 Banks and Blackstone announced financing for an SPV to purchase AI chips and network equipment. Reuters reported around US$43.5bn first-lien senior debt, with second-lien capital involving Blackstone and residual-value support from Broadcom. Reuters Classification: Financing arrangement, not an ordinary unsecured corporate bond. Coupon, all-in yield and individual loan maturities were not disclosed. Oracle: attempts to cap future funding requirements Reuters · 28 October 2026 Oracle said it expects to need up to US$20bn of additional financing for the remainder of fiscal 2027, split between debt and equity. It reported US$125.34bn in notes payable and other borrowings as of 31 August. Its goal is positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028. Reuters Classification: Funding plan and management forecast, not a newly issued US$20bn bond. Two additional transactions deserve attention: Reuters reported that SpaceX secured US$40bn of chip-related debt financing with an Apollo affiliate on 26 October, while Argentum AI was only in talks for a proposed US$5bn chip financing deal on 27 October. These must not be counted as equally completed borrowing events. Reuters Moody's also told Reuters on 27 October that 17% of 607 borrowers in its tracked sample used payment-in-kind interest, while the 2027–2029 refinancing period remained a concern for weaker borrowers. Reuters 4. New issuance and borrowing monitor The table below uses actual final pricing term sheets wherever available. These are issue-date terms, not live secondary-market yields. All amounts USD. Issue price is per 100 of face value. UST benchmark yield and issue spread are quoted together. N/V = not verified in the reviewed source. Issuer / pricing date Amount · Maturity Coupon Issue price Issue YTM UST benchmark yield / spread United Rentals · 26 Oct $700m · 15 Oct 2029 5.550% 99.922 5.580% 4.780% / +80bp United Rentals · 26 Oct $800m · 15 Oct 2031 5.750% 99.884 5.778% 4.828% / +95bp United Rentals · 26 Oct $1bn · 15 Oct 2036 6.200% 99.710 6.240% 4.990% / +125bp Texas Instruments · 26 Oct $500m · 9 Nov 2028 5.000% 99.827 5.092% 4.712% / +38bp Texas Instruments · 26 Oct $500m · 9 Nov 2031 5.350% 99.779 5.401% 4.821% / +58bp CBRE Services · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2032 5.650% 99.424 5.782% 4.832% / +95bp CBRE Services · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2037 5.900% 97.872 6.186% 4.986% / +120bp Main Street Capital · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2030 6.550% 99.258 6.800% 4.800% / +200bp KeyCorp · 27 Oct $1bn · 2 Nov 2032 5.889% initially 100.000 5.889% initial fixed pricing 4.839% / +105bp Sources: Original SEC/issuer pricing documents. sec.gov +4 Special point on KeyCorp: Its coupon becomes floating for the final year, at compounded SOFR +130bp. The quoted 5.889% fixed-rate pricing figure is not a guaranteed fixed YTM across the entire note's life. Ratings and financing purposes Issuer Credit ratings verified Borrowing structure / purpose United Rentals Moody's Baa3 / S&P BBB− Senior unsecured; specific proceeds not verified in pricing sheet Texas Instruments N/V in reviewed term sheet Senior notes linked to an acquisition, with special mandatory redemption provisions CBRE Services Moody's Baa1 / S&P BBB+ / Fitch BBB+ Senior unsecured; general corporate purposes, including commercial-paper repayment and acquisition-related uses Main Street Capital S&P BBB− / Fitch BBB− BDC unsecured notes; initially repay revolving-credit borrowing KeyCorp N/V in reviewed term sheet Fixed-to-floating senior bank debt Microsoft N/V in preliminary prospectus Proposed senior unsecured debt; general corporate purposes including capital requirements Anthropic-related SPV N/V Senior and second-lien AI-equipment financing SpaceX-related financing N/V Chip-related debt, as reported by Reuters SEC +4 What the pricing tells us The verified spread dispersion is substantial: Spread on newly priced USD debt Spread above each deal's stated Treasury benchmark. Issue-date spreads, not live OAS. 0bp 55bp 110bp 165bp 220bp Texas Instruments 2… Texas Instruments 2… United Rentals 2029 CBRE 2032 KeyCorp 2032 CBRE 2037 United Rentals 2036 Main Street Capital… Texas Instruments 2028: Issue spread 38bp Texas Instruments 2031: Issue spread 58bp United Rentals 2029: Issue spread 80bp CBRE 2032: Issue spread 95bp KeyCorp 2032: Issue spread 105bp CBRE 2037: Issue spread 120bp United Rentals 2036: Issue spread 125bp Main Street Capital 2030: Issue spread 200bp Selected issuance spreads sourced from final pricing term sheets above. Different maturities, issuer risk, capital structures and investor liquidity make this a descriptive comparison rather than a pure credit-risk ranking. Main Street Capital's +200bp spread is particularly noteworthy beside the relatively small issuance concessions for Texas Instruments. But the higher spread is not simply free income. A BDC owns portfolios of loans to businesses and its own funding conditions reflect both asset quality and financing risk. For context, Main Street says proceeds will initially refinance existing revolving facilities. That illustrates an important distinction between gross debt issuance and net additional borrowing. 5. Loan delinquencies, defaults and late-payment watch Latest verified national household dataset New York Fed Q2 2026, published 11 August 2026. Full 46-page original report: Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, Q2 2026. The most recent comprehensive quarter verified is June 2026. These numbers should not be labelled October delinquency observations. Total household debt $18.771tn Balances in some stage of delinquency 4.7% New transitions into serious delinquency: 90+ days Loan category Q2 2025 Q2 2026 Change Mortgages 1.29% 1.52% +0.23pp Credit cards 6.93% 6.97% +0.04pp Auto loans 2.93% 3.00% +0.07pp Home-equity lines 1.15% 1.15% 0.00pp Student loans 12.88% 7.83% −5.05pp These are annualised flows into serious delinquency, not percentages of total outstanding balances already 90+ days past due. Student-loan comparisons remain affected by reporting changes associated with payment resumption. FEDERAL RESERVE BANK of NEW YORK Where to inspect earlier warning signals in the full report Indicator New York Fed report Balances 30, 60, 90 and 120+ days late Page 11 Percent of balances 90+ days delinquent by category Page 12 Transitions into 30+ day delinquency Page 13 Transitions into 90+ day delinquency Page 14 Current mortgages becoming 30–60 days late Page 15 Mortgages already 30–60 days late that recover or worsen Page 16 The underlying charts are available, but the retrieved report does not disclose precise current numerical endpoints for every 30- and 60-day series. I have not inferred exact values from a graph. ReportData_template One additional datapoint is important: 10.6% of student-loan balances were already 90+ days overdue in Q2 2026, up from 10.3% in Q1. That is a stock measure, distinct from the annualised transition figure above. ReportData_template Private credit, PIK and defaults Credit stress signal Verified observation Data period / limitation Moody's tracked borrowers using PIK interest 17% of 607 borrowers Reported 27 Oct Fitch-rated BDC realised losses 0.5% First half 2026, not full year Moody's modelled default probability: public BDCs About 0.49% June 2026, forecast probability, not realised default Moody's modelled default probability: Baa corporates About 0.25% June 2026, different credit universe Moody's reported PIK income share of public BDCs Approximately 8% Compared with about 5.5% in 2021 Redemption requests at some non-traded vehicles Approximately 10.5% Spring 2026, limited sample Reuters +2 The 17% figure does not mean 17% have defaulted. PIK is an interest-payment arrangement. It may support liquidity temporarily but can increase outstanding debt and create refinancing pressure. Moody's also estimated a 2025 private-credit default range of 1.6–4.7%, depending on treatment of distressed exchanges and the relevant sample. It is not directly comparable with the modelled BDC probabilities in the table. Moody's Commercial real estate and bank loans The FDIC's Q2 2026 banking profile graph book remains a useful official source for noncurrent loans, past-due and nonaccrual balances, charge-offs, CRE and bank-lending categories. FDIC Q2 2026 Quarterly Banking Profile Graph Book I could verify the underlying Q2 2026 reporting period but not a complete current set of CRE delinquency percentages from the retrieved pages. Consequently, no unsupported point estimates are presented. Distinguishing types of credit deterioration Status What it actually means 30 days late An early contractual payment delay 60 days late A more persistent arrears problem 90+ days late Serious delinquency, not necessarily a completed default event Nonaccrual Lender no longer recognises interest on the usual accrual basis PIK interest Interest added to debt or paid through additional securities Distressed exchange A restructuring that can count as default under rating-agency definitions Payment default A borrower misses a contractual obligation, subject to relevant grace periods Bankruptcy A legal restructuring or insolvency process Charge-off A lender recognises a loan loss in its accounts Watch point: The strongest warning is not one isolated high delinquency rate. It is a sequence in which new arrears rise, cure rates deteriorate, interest capitalisation grows and refinancing becomes less available. 6. Duration, spread and leveraged-margin scenarios All calculations below are hypothetical risk illustrations, not valuations of any client holdings. They exclude coupon accrual, financing interest, fees, FX changes and changes in bank asset recognition. Scenario A: Long Treasury yield shocks Assume a hypothetical 30-year Treasury exposure with modified duration of 16 and convexity of 300. A 2041 Treasury, 2044 Treasury and STRIP maturing in 2054 would have different sensitivities. Treasury change Credit-spread change Total yield change Estimated price move 0bp +100bp +100bp −6.700% +50bp +50bp +100bp −6.700% +50bp +100bp +150bp −9.825% +100bp +100bp +200bp −12.800% For the +150bp scenario: − 7 ( 0.015 ) + 1 2 ( 60 ) ( 0.015 ) 2 = − 0.09825 −7(0.015)+ 2 1 ​ (60)(0.015) 2 =−0.09825 Credit spread and Treasury movements are kept distinct before combining their effect on price. Scenario C: Hypothetical leveraged Treasury investment Assume, for demonstration only: Item Value Initial bond market value US$1,000,000 Loan outstanding US$700,000 Initial investor equity US$300,000 Illustrative maximum LTV 75% Starting borrowing headroom US$50,000 This 75% LTV is not an OCBC lending rule or security-specific recognition rate. Borrowing headroom formula: 𝐻 = 0.75 × Bond Market Value − 700 , 000 H=0.75×Bond Market Value−700,000 Yield shock Bond value Investor equity Borrowing headroom −50bp $1,083,750 $383,750 +$112,812.50 No change $1,000,000 $300,000 +$50,000 +50bp $923,750 $223,750 −$7,187.50 +100bp $855,000 $155,000 −$58,750 At +100bp, the investor has an estimated US$145,000 mark-to-market equity loss and a US$58,750 shortfall against the illustrative LTV threshold. A negative headroom figure is the collateral shortfall under these assumptions. It does not mean the investor's equity is negative. For a CHF-financed portfolio, the actual outcome would also depend on CHF loan balance, accrued interest, collateral-recognition rules and CHF/USD movements. None of those personal inputs have been invented. 7. Strategy, risks and actionable watchlist Risk Current reading Portfolio action Long Treasury duration 30Y yield 5.32% Stage exposure and quantify DV01/convexity IG credit Index OAS 86bp Demand adequate spread for issuer and liquidity risk HY credit Index OAS 314bp Separate broad spread tightening from distressed issuer cases AI infrastructure debt Large SPV and equipment financing Map borrower, guarantor, tenant and collateral separately Private-credit maturity wall Moody's highlights 2027–2029 Review debt maturity ladders and interest coverage PIK / nonaccrual Growing relevance in weaker credit Track cash interest received versus accounting income CRE and consumer late payments Mixed Q2 household trends Monitor progression from 30-day to 90+ delinquency Leveraged portfolios Large downside sensitivity under yield shocks Preserve collateral headroom and unencumbered liquidity For a Singapore private-banking portfolio, the practical priority is to avoid treating yield, coupon, carry, unrealised P&L and borrowing capacity as interchangeable numbers. A bond yielding 6.8% with a 200bp issuance spread is a fundamentally different exposure from a Treasury yielding 5.32%, even if both are USD-denominated. Once funded through a CHF loan, there is a further layer of collateral and FX risk. 8. Research appendix: original source links The first group prioritises full papers, original statistical reports and substantive primary research. More than ten directly linked sources are included. Older studies are identified so a paper from September cannot quietly masquerade as this week's discovery. Primary research and white papers # Title · Publisher · Date Direct source and research relevance 1 Building AI on Credit: Structures and Spillovers · BIS · 27 Oct 2026 Full paper, PDF (8 pages). AI debt architecture, leases, duration supply and financial stability. Graphs 1–3. 2 Building AI on Credit: Online Annex · BIS · 27 Oct 2026 Technical annex, PDF. Event-study regression results, robustness and underlying event definitions. 3 Bank Liquidity Regulation and the Growth of Private Credit · BIS · 20 Oct 2026 Working Paper 1388, PDF (48 pages). Empirical evidence on lending migrating from banks to private credit. Prior-week paper. 4 North America Data Center Roundup: Fourth-Quarter 2026 · S&P Global Ratings · 16 Oct 2026 Original S&P report. Project finance, corporate and structured-finance data. Full-text access may require registration. 5 S&P Global Ratings Launches Interactive North America Data Center Dashboard · S&P · 23 Oct 2026 Original research release. US$105.3bn rated issuance and transaction mix; links to the interactive dashboard. 6 Domestic and Foreign Insurer Corporate Bond Demand and Monetary Policy · Bank of England · 9 Oct 2026 Working Paper 1210, PDF (59 pages). Insurer demand, cross-border bond flows and duration. Infrastructure leasing, tenant quality and long-term debt repayment risks. Final investment assessment Three observations stand out. First, Treasury duration and corporate credit should not be conflated. A 30-year government bond can lose substantial market value without any credit deterioration, while an IG corporate issuer may face additional spread widening. Second, AI debt is increasingly being transformed through project vehicles, equipment collateral and financial guarantees. The borrower, asset owner, customer and ultimate risk-bearer may be different entities. The BIS and S&P research make that distinction particularly important. Third, the credit cycle should be monitored through cash payments, not only ratings and quoted yields. Rising PIK utilisation, weakening loan cures, higher nonaccruals and refinancing dependence can reveal deterioration before headline defaults rise. For bond positioning: Preserve liquidity and collateral headroom, accumulate long duration selectively, favour transparent credit structures, and require meaningful compensation for subordinated or illiquid exposures. For client conversations: A higher coupon is not the same as a safer investment. The relevant question is whether the borrower can continue paying and whether the investor can hold the security through volatility without being forced to sell. The highest-priority reading this week is the BIS 27 October AI debt paper, followed by the S&P 23 October data-centre research, the BIS private-credit working paper, and the actual SEC pricing sheets, which show what borrowers are genuinely paying for capital rather than what a news headline suggests. entries.title: SPY closed-trade review: premium captured and risk released
entries.text: call-spy-closed-review-20261105 SPY 2026-11-05 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z Historical closed-trade review Seven closed round trips reconciled to US$446 of gross trading P/L in the reviewed order-chain screenshots. The six short-put trades contributed US$417 and the separate short-call trade contributed US$29. This is a screenshot-based reconciliation, not a broker statement or independently audited track record. SPY closed-trade review: premium captured and risk released 2026-11-05T06:22:19Z 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z public Historical closed round trips; expiries differ Approved redacted summary of the dated private report. Original account evidence is not published. Summary Seven closed round trips reconciled to US$446 of gross trading P/L in the reviewed order-chain screenshots. The six short-put trades contributed US$417 and the separate short-call trade contributed US$29. This is a screenshot-based reconciliation, not a broker statement or independently audited track record. Visual 1: Profit bridge US$1,376 opening credits - US$930 closing buybacks = US$446 gross P/L. Chart: opening credits in blue, buybacks in amber and gross profit in green. Label 32.41% as the proportion of opening credit retained, not return on account equity or return on margin. Visual 2: Closed-trade ledger All expiries below are in 2026. Prices are per share, with a 100-share contract multiplier. | Option | Contracts | Sold | Bought back | Gross P/L | Opening credit captured | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | US$600 put, 31 December | 2 | US$1.73 | US$1.04 | +US$138 | 39.88% | | US$635 put, 31 December | 2 | US$2.15 | US$1.53 | +US$124 | 28.84% | | US$590 put, 31 December | 1 | US$1.55 | US$0.94 | +US$61 | 39.35% | | US$590 put, 4 December | 1 | US$0.64 | US$0.35 | +US$29 | 45.31% | | US$600 put, 4 December | 1 | US$0.72 | US$0.39 | +US$33 | 45.83% | | US$595 put, 4 December | 1 | US$0.69 | US$0.37 | +US$32 | 46.38% | | US$805 call, 18 December | 1 | US$2.40 | US$2.11 | +US$29 | 12.08% | | Total | 9 contracts across 7 round trips | | | +US$446 | 32.41% overall | Why close early? The six puts captured 28.84% to 46.38% of their starting credit in approximately 27 to 50 hours. Buying them back crystallised US$417 of gross put gains and ended those positions' future assignment exposure. Pursuing the remaining US$719 of put premium would have kept downside and margin risk open. The US$805 call was a separate, later trade and captured only 12.08% of its starting credit. It opened after the puts had closed. It must not be described as part of a simultaneous short-strangle position, and an uncovered short call can have unlimited upside loss. Visual 3: Risk diagram Eight short puts → 800 shares on full assignment → US$484,500 combined strike purchase obligation. A hypothetical additional US$50 fall per assigned share → 800 × US$50 = US$40,000 further share-price loss. Use three separately labelled boxes: assignment purchase obligation, broker margin requirement and discretionary downside reserve. Do not add them together as though they were the same thing. Margin and evidence limits The exact return on margin cannot be established from these screenshots. Historical peak broker buying-power reduction is missing. Do not use the earlier ten-put proposal's buying-power figure for the different executed trades, and do not add the later call's requirement to the puts' peak as though they overlapped. These listed trades were already closed at the review date. Hypothetical hold-to-expiry figures are counterfactuals, not outstanding positions or promises of further income. Gross P/L excludes fees, financing and taxes not identifiable in the screenshots. Account balances and raw broker screenshots are not included in this public summary. entries.title: SPY short-put comparison: income versus assignment obligation
entries.text: call-spy-put-comparison-20261103 SPY 2026-11-03 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z Hypothetical strategy comparison The higher-premium package carried a much larger purchase obligation. The two historical sell-to-open tickets compared one SPY US$700 put with ten SPY US$600 puts. They were order illustrations, not confirmed executions, and the maturities differed. SPY short-put comparison: income versus assignment obligation 2026-11-03T08:19:13Z 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z public 2026-11-03 Historical option snapshot and scenario analysis Approved redacted summary of the dated private report. Original account evidence is not published. Summary The higher-premium package carried a much larger purchase obligation. The two historical sell-to-open tickets compared one SPY US$700 put with ten SPY US$600 puts. They were order illustrations, not confirmed executions, and the maturities differed. Visual 1: Side-by-side contract table | Measure | Strategy A: one US$700 put | Strategy B: ten US$600 puts | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Expiry | 26 February 2027 | 31 December 2026 | | Days shown on the original ticket | 115 | 58 | | Assumed premium per share | US$12.19 | US$1.88 | | Maximum gross premium | US$1,219 | US$1,880 | | Shares if all assigned | 100 | 1,000 | | Gross assignment obligation | US$70,000 | US$600,000 | | Expiry break-even per share | US$687.81 | US$598.12 | | Maximum option loss if SPY reaches zero | US$68,781 | US$598,120 | | Premium / full assignment obligation | 1.7414% | 0.3133% | Chart: pair gross premium bars with separate assignment-obligation bars. Use separate labelled axes so the additional US$661 premium is not visually confused with the additional US$530,000 obligation. What the comparison means Strategy A was an ownership-oriented illustration; Strategy B was a leveraged premium-harvesting illustration. The first structure requires willingness and funding to buy 100 shares at the strike. The ten-put structure can create a US$600,000 purchase obligation even when the initial buying-power requirement is much lower. The reported tenor for Strategy B was 58 days, not roughly 40 days. Preserve the 31 December 2026 expiry and the ticket's displayed day count. Do not compare the two premiums as though they were earned over the same period. Visual 2: Downside payoff table | SPY at each option's own expiry | Strategy A P/L | Strategy B P/L | | --- | ---: | ---: | | US$700 | +US$1,219 | +US$1,880 | | US$650 | -US$3,781 | +US$1,880 | | US$600 | -US$8,781 | +US$1,880 | | US$550 | -US$13,781 | -US$48,120 | | US$500 | -US$18,781 | -US$98,120 | Chart: labelled payoff lines, with an explicit warning that the expiries differ. These are terminal scenarios, not interim option marks. Risks and limits Buying-power effect is not maximum loss and is not guaranteed to remain fixed. A fall in SPY or a rise in implied volatility can increase short-option losses and margin demands before expiry. Early assignment and forced liquidation are possible. All returns are conditional and before costs. The original quote reference was SPY US$751.96. The assumed limit premiums do not prove that either trade filled. The report makes no claim about current availability, current pricing or personal account balances. entries.title: QQQ hedge update: partial protection through a sharper selloff
entries.text: call-qqq-hedge-review-20261031 QQQ 2026-10-31 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z Hypothetical hedge review The working eight-put example showed an indicative gain of US$14,216, not a confirmed trading profit. The analysis used eight QQQ US$750 puts expiring 19 February 2027, a reconstructed reference premium of US$46.50 and the later displayed bid of US$64.27. Entry and exit fills were not established. QQQ hedge update: partial protection through a sharper selloff 2026-10-31T03:57:36Z 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z public Historical option snapshot and scenario analysis Approved redacted summary of the dated private report. Original account evidence is not published. Summary The working eight-put example showed an indicative gain of US$14,216, not a confirmed trading profit. The analysis used eight QQQ US$750 puts expiring 19 February 2027, a reconstructed reference premium of US$46.50 and the later displayed bid of US$64.27. Entry and exit fills were not established. Visual 1: Three-stage quote and valuation table | Measure | Initial reference | 30 October review | 31 October update | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | QQQ snapshot | US$721.25 | US$715.28 | US$690.53 | | Put premium per share | US$46.50 reconstructed | US$51.96 bid | US$64.27 bid | | Eight-contract value | US$37,200 | US$41,568 | US$51,416 | | Conditional gain | US$0 | +US$4,368 | +US$14,216 | Chart: use three separate labelled observations, not a continuous live-price series. Reference cost is reconstructed; later values are indicative bid-side marks. Purpose and outcome The plan was temporary protection through an earnings window, with an intended exit one week after entry. A longer option expiry was chosen to reduce estimated short-holding-period time decay. The stated purpose was protection against a repricing associated with AI capital spending, cash-flow pressure and debt-service concerns, rather than a claim that a particular company would fail. The later update showed a larger dollar gain but a smaller proportion of the illustrative stock loss offset. The report's QQQ-equivalent portfolio comparison showed 47.68% of the reference loss offset, versus 75.39% in the earlier review. Actual stock holdings and their returns were not established. Visual 2: Normalized hedge comparison Normalize the stock sleeve to 100 reference units. Fund the option premium separately at 5.3143 units, so both cases start with 105.3143 total units. | At the 31 October snapshot | Without hedge | With the assumed puts | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Stock-sleeve change | -4.2593 units | -4.2593 units | | Hedge contribution | 0.0000 units | +2.0309 units | | Combined change | -4.2593 units | -2.2284 units | | Stock loss offset | 0.00% | 47.68% | Chart: two loss bars, with the hedge contribution shown as a green bridge. Label this a normalized hypothetical portfolio, not personal account performance. Costs and limitations Time decay was one component of cost, not a fixed insurance bill. Starting Greeks suggested approximately US$660 of seven-day theta for the eight-put example if price and implied volatility were unchanged. Price moves, volatility changes, bid-ask spreads and execution costs could produce very different results. These snapshots do not establish a completed one-week hedge or a realized return. The latest midpoint would imply a US$14,908 gain, but midpoint is not an assured fill. Fees, financing, dividends, tax and slippage are excluded, and a QQQ proxy cannot establish the performance of a different stock portfolio. entries.title: Three questions before any market headline
entries.text: starting-point Three questions before any market headline Start here Ask what is happening in the economy, what is already priced into investments, and what reaches your own pocket. These reports become easier to understand once the three questions are kept separate. The economy describes activity, jobs and prices. Markets put a price today on an uncertain future. Your personal outcome also depends on the price you paid, the currency you spend, fees, financing and when you need your money back. Strong growth can coexist with a disappointing investment return if buyers already paid for even better growth. A highly rated borrower can issue a bond whose market price swings sharply. An overseas portfolio can gain in its own currency yet deliver a much smaller gain in SGD. These are different mechanisms, so a single green or red headline is usually inadequate. Use the MAS October review to understand Singapore’s current growth, inflation and policy backdrop. Use JPMorgan to explain global markets and investment mechanics. Use MAS, GIC and Temasek annual reports to understand institutional roles and measurement. The three supplied written reports are secondary analyses: their claims need the underlying official sources. The reading order in this briefing follows those links. It moves from growth and inflation to equities, rates and credit, then currency, public finances, institutions and private markets. All quoted numbers retain the source’s own displayed precision. A source-published rounded figure is not converted into a falsely exact economic measurement. A useful market update explains a cause, a possible consequence and a decision to monitor. It should help the reader ask a better question. The review date of this briefing is 31 October 2026. The charts are dated snapshots, not live prices or a claim that all figures describe the same day. Begin each client discussion with spending currency, time horizon, cash needs and ability to withstand a temporary loss. mas-macro jpm-markets jpm-alternatives Explanation with dated evidence

entries.title: Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven
entries.text: singapore-growth Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven Singapore Technology is doing much of the heavy lifting; a strong national figure does not mean every sector is thriving. The MAS October review reports Q3 2026 GDP growth of 5.4% year on year and 1.1% quarter on quarter after seasonal adjustment. These are advance estimates. The two figures answer different questions: the first compares with the same quarter a year earlier; the second compares with the immediately preceding quarter after removing recurring seasonal patterns. Technology-related industries accounted for around 75% of year-on-year growth in Q3, according to MAS. That is a share of the increase in output, not a claim that technology is 75% of Singapore’s economy. The same page identifies technology-related industries as 22.1% of nominal value added in 2025. Confusing the level of activity with its contribution to growth would substantially overstate the sector’s size. The practical picture is an uneven expansion. Electronics, machinery, related trade and information services benefit from AI investment. Other parts of the economy face different demand and cost conditions. MAS describes weakness in some consumer-facing businesses and pressure on oil-related industries even while the headline economy expands. MAS expects the technology expansion to continue into 2027 at a more measured pace. This is its baseline assessment, not a promise. A slowdown in growth means output is rising less quickly; it does not automatically mean a recession. The vulnerability is that a narrower engine leaves the economy more exposed if AI spending or its financing disappoints. Think of a company whose best division generates most of the additional profit. The company can be growing strongly while other divisions struggle. Do not treat strong GDP as a buy signal for every Singapore company, property or fund. Sector earnings, balance sheets and prices still differ. Watch whether growth broadens beyond technology, whether semiconductor orders hold up, and whether jobs and household spending follow. mas-macro mas-oct2026-p21 Published observations and MAS outlook

entries.title: Why MAS cares about the SGD basket
entries.text: inflation-sgd Why MAS cares about the SGD basket Singapore Singapore uses the exchange rate to help control imported inflation; USD/SGD is only one part of that policy picture. MAS Core Inflation rose from 1.5% in Q2 2026 to 2.1% in July–August. The October review forecasts core inflation of 1.5–2.0% for 2026 and 1.5–2.5% for 2027. These are forecasts for annual averages, not a ceiling on every monthly reading. Core inflation excludes accommodation and private transport; it is not identical to a particular household’s cost-of-living change. Inflation describes how fast prices rise. If inflation slows, prices can still be increasing. It is the difference between climbing stairs more slowly and going back downstairs. Energy, food, transport, wages, subsidies and competition can move differently, so the components matter as much as the headline. MAS maintained the prevailing appreciation rate of the S$NEER policy band in October 2026, after tightening in April and July. S$NEER is a trade-weighted currency measure. The bilateral USD/SGD rate is the price of one currency against another. An appreciating basket can coexist with SGD weakness against a particular currency, because the other basket currencies also move. For households, a stronger SGD can soften imported costs. For an investor with unhedged overseas assets, it can reduce the value translated back into SGD. Those effects can occur together. MAS’s policy objective concerns price stability in Singapore; maximising the SGD accounting return on foreign reserves is a different objective. The review’s inflation research separates external demand, external supply and domestic forces. It estimates that external factors explain about 68% of the inflation variation captured by its model over the sample. That is a model-based historical decomposition, not a statement that 68% of each household bill is imported. The policy implications depend on the source and persistence of the shock. The same stronger dollar that makes some imported goods cheaper can make an overseas investment look smaller on an SGD statement. A fall in USD/SGD alone does not measure the full MAS policy stance. Neither the basket path nor the inflation forecast guarantees a particular future FX rate. Separate a household’s SGD cash requirements from long-term foreign assets. Read the latest policy decision alongside inflation components and actual bilateral rates. mas-macro mas-oct2026-p10 mas-oct2026-p29 Published data and labelled forecasts

entries.title: Who pays for the AI buildout
entries.text: ai-financing Who pays for the AI buildout Equities Demand can be strong while the bill for future capacity rises even faster than cash generation. JPMorgan’s page 22 groups Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. It shows total company capital expenditure of US$416 billion in 2025, with consensus forecasts of US$799 billion in 2026, US$1,093 billion in 2027 and US$1,200 billion in 2028. The last three are forecasts. The measure is total company capex, not a directly measured AI-only spending total. Operating cash flow is cash generated from running a business. Capital expenditure pays for long-lived assets such as equipment and buildings. On the slide, free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex. A company can report accounting profit while free cash flow is weak because it is spending heavily on future capacity. That does not by itself prove insolvency, but it changes the funding question. MAS provides a useful second view. Page 23 compares semiconductor production conditions with a composite indicator of hyperscalers’ capacity to sustain capex. The latter considers cash-flow margins, leverage and investment intensity. Its company universe differs from JPMorgan’s and includes CoreWeave. These are analytical indices, not an observable default probability or a reproducible bank credit score. The connection is straightforward: suppliers can enjoy strong orders today while customers take on larger financing commitments. If future AI revenue justifies the spending, the expansion may endure. If monetisation disappoints, buyers may reduce capex, lenders may demand better terms and suppliers may face weaker orders. MAS describes this as a downside risk, while judging near-term backlogs and commitments supportive. For a portfolio, inspect the shared economic exposure. Technology equities, semiconductor suppliers, data-centre property, power infrastructure and private credit to the same ecosystem may all respond to one investment cycle. Different product labels do not ensure different underlying risks. A restaurant can be busy and profitable while borrowing heavily to open many new outlets. The question is whether the new outlets eventually earn enough to justify the cost. Large capex is neither proof of a bubble nor proof of an attractive investment. Aggregate cash-flow charts cannot establish whether an individual borrower can service its debts. Track cash generation against capex, debt and lease commitments, refinancing needs, customer contracts and actual monetisation. Keep each issuer’s analysis separate. jpm-markets mas-macro jpm-gtm-p22 mas-oct2026-p23 Historical observations, forecasts and risk analysis

entries.title: Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly
entries.text: equity-concentration Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly Equities An index can own many names while a small group still drives much of its value. At 30 September 2026, JPMorgan shows the ten largest S&P 500 constituents at 40.6% of market capitalisation and 36.1% of trailing earnings. A market-cap-weighted index puts more money into larger companies. Counting the number of holdings therefore does not tell you how evenly the risk is spread. The earnings share also matters. The largest companies contribute substantial profits as well as substantial market value. Concentration alone does not prove prices are irrational. It tells you which companies and business drivers can most influence results, and where earnings disappointment could be consequential. JPMorgan’s valuation page reports a forward P/E of 19.0 times against its 30-year average of 17.2 times. Forward P/E is price divided by forecast earnings. A higher ratio means paying more for each unit of expected profit. If the earnings forecast changes, the valuation can change even without a move in the share price. CAPE, also shown in the guide, uses a long historical average of inflation-adjusted earnings. It is a different measurement, so its number should not be compared directly with forward P/E as if one were an alternative price quote. Valuation measures help frame expectations; they do not provide a date for a market correction. For a Singapore investor, add a currency lens. A U.S. index chart generally describes the U.S. market in USD. The return in SGD depends on the exchange rate and any hedging. Owning an S&P 500 fund, a technology fund and several megacap shares may add overlapping exposure rather than meaningful new diversification. A supermarket basket with hundreds of items can still be dominated by a few expensive purchases. The number of items does not determine where most of the money went. A historical average is not a fair-value guarantee. Concentration can persist, and expensive markets can keep rising. Review the largest underlying holdings across all funds and direct shares. Compare business drivers, regions, currencies and valuation assumptions before adding another product. jpm-markets jpm-gtm-p8 jpm-gtm-p5 30 September 2026 snapshot

entries.title: Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond
entries.text: bond-duration Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond Bonds Credit quality concerns repayment; duration concerns how much the price moves when required yields change. A fixed-rate bond promises a stream of payments. If comparable new bonds offer a higher yield, buyers usually pay less for the old payment stream. If required yields fall, the old stream becomes more attractive. The issuer can remain financially sound throughout this repricing. Maturity is the date principal is due. Duration measures sensitivity to a change in yield. A long maturity and low coupon often leave more of a bond’s value dependent on distant payments, increasing its rate sensitivity. Convexity describes the bend in the price–yield relationship; it explains why a simple straight-line estimate becomes less accurate for larger moves. JPMorgan page 34 illustrates total-return scenarios under a parallel shift in the yield curve. The printed figures below show how the range widens at longer maturities. The slide does not explicitly state the scenario horizon, so these should be described as the publisher’s illustrations, not independently verified one-year forecasts. Long yields are influenced by more than the next central-bank meeting. Inflation expectations, the compensation for holding long debt, government borrowing needs and supply can all matter. MAS’s October financial-conditions chapter describes rising long government yields even alongside resilient equity markets. Holding to maturity changes the decision if contractual payments are met and the investor can hold. It does not remove inflation, currency, funding or collateral risk. A financed investor might be forced to sell before maturity, turning an interim price fall into a realised loss. This is why duration must be assessed together with liquidity and borrowing terms. A reliable tenant does not make the resale price of a long rental contract stable when market rents and interest rates change. These publisher illustrations are not prices or P&L forecasts for a specific Temasek or Treasury holding. They exclude the investor’s own FX, fees, financing and margin arrangements. Compare duration and maturity separately. Stress the relevant part of the curve, and check the cash and collateral available to survive the path. jpm-markets mas-macro jpm-gtm-p34 mas-oct2026-p9 Treasury maturity Yield falls 1 percentage point No yield change Yield rises 1 percentage point 2 years 6.8% 4.9% 3.0% 10 years 13.1% 5.3% −2.5% 30 years 20.3% 5.6% −9.0% Exact displayed scenario values from JPMorgan page 34. Parallel curve shift; the slide does not explicitly identify the scenario horizon. These are source illustrations, not an investor-specific simulation. Publisher illustrative scenarios

entries.title: Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk
entries.text: credit-spread Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk Bonds A bond can offer a high total yield while paying only a small extra amount for the company’s credit risk. A useful breakdown is a government or near-risk-free reference yield plus compensation for credit, liquidity and other bond features. This is a pricing guide, not an exact universal identity. Credit spread is not the coupon and not the entire yield. One basis point equals 0.01 percentage point. JPMorgan page 36 shows investment-grade option-adjusted spreads of 80 basis points versus a 144 basis-point long-run average in its chart. High-yield spreads are 311 basis points versus 498. Yet displayed yields to worst are 6.0% and 8.3%. Much of the attractive-looking yield therefore comes from the wider interest-rate environment, while the extra credit compensation is relatively narrow. This distinction matters when deciding between taking more duration and taking weaker credit. They expose the portfolio to different problems. Government yields can rise even if an issuer’s business is healthy. Credit spreads can widen even if government yields are unchanged. Both can happen together. An average spread does not establish the value of an individual bond. Seniority, covenants, cash flows, refinancing dates, liquidity and recovery prospects differ. The default chart on the same JPMorgan slide also uses different treatment of distressed exchanges across some categories. A reader should retain that methodology rather than turning the chart into a simple ranking of all default risks. The base rental market can be expensive even when the extra rent for accepting a troublesome tenant is small. Total income and compensation for a particular risk are different questions. Tight spreads do not prove an imminent sell-off. High yield does not guarantee a sufficient cushion against defaults or spread widening. Compare the extra yield with the specific risk being accepted. For each issuer, examine cash coverage, maturity schedule, debt structure and the liquidity available to exit. jpm-markets jpm-gtm-p36 30 September 2026 snapshot Investment grade High yield Option-adjusted spread 80 bps 311 bps Long-run average in chart 144 bps 498 bps Displayed yield to worst 6.0% 8.3% Figures retain the source’s displayed precision. The long-run averages use the chart’s historical window, not a promised normal level. Dated credit-market observations

entries.title: Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD
entries.text: fx-return Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD Currency The investment return and the currency conversion multiply; they do not simply subtract. Define the exchange rate as SGD received for one USD. If an investment’s USD value changes by r and this exchange rate changes by f over the same measurement period, a simplified return with no intermediate external flows is (1 + r) × (1 + f) − 1 in SGD. This convention matters: quoting the inverse exchange rate changes the calculation. The supplied USD sensitivity report uses a 5.60% USD return and a 3.00% annual USD decline against SGD over a matched annualised horizon. The exact arithmetic is 1.056 × 0.97 − 1 = 0.02432 = 2.432%. The original report displayed 2.43% because it explicitly rounded to two decimal places. This briefing preserves the exact computed value. There is a major interpretation limit. GIC’s 5.6% is a historical twenty-year annualised USD return, not a next-year forecast. Pairing it with assumed future FX weakness is a conditional illustration. It does not reveal GIC’s direct net USD position, currency hedges or an expected future SGD return. Changing the reporting currency of a diversified global portfolio is also different from measuring how much the portfolio is economically exposed to one currency. Non-USD assets can themselves rise in USD terms when USD weakens. Company revenues, costs, borrowing and hedging can pull in different directions. For an actual bond portfolio, coupon payment dates, conversion rates, fees and financing cash flows require their own dated ledger. A simple terminal-return identity should not be used to silently approximate those flows. For a household, the relevant question remains what purchasing power is available in the currency of future spending. The investment can grow in dollars while each dollar buys fewer Singapore dollars. Both steps affect the final SGD result. The 3% FX move is a stated scenario from the supplied analysis, not a forecast by MAS. The institutional reports do not disclose enough to estimate a precise common USD sensitivity for MAS, GIC and Temasek. Show investment P&L, income, FX effects, fees and financing separately, then reconcile them. Match the currency and horizon before comparing returns. gic-2026 mas-2026 temasek-2026 Assumed annual USD weakening USD return assumption Exact converted SGD return 0% 5.60% 5.6% 1% 5.60% 4.544% 2% 5.60% 3.488% 3% 5.60% 2.432% 4% 5.60% 1.376% 5% 5.60% 0.32% Derived from inputs already shown in supplied Report 2. Assumes matched annualised horizons; not a forecast, institutional exposure estimate or bond/loan simulation. Explicit conditional arithmetic

entries.title: Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from
entries.text: public-finances Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from Singapore Taxes and other operating revenue are one stream; the permitted investment-return contribution is another. A household analogy helps: recurring earnings fund spending, while accumulated savings can also generate income. Singapore’s system has a specific constitutional framework, so the analogy should not be taken as an exact household budget. The important distinction is between the reserve principal, investment returns and the amount available for annual spending. The audited FY2025/26 government accounts show operating revenue of S$130,049,822,095.34 and Net Investment Returns Contribution of S$27,522,875,864.50. Adding those two reported values gives S$157,572,697,959.84. This sum describes revenue before deducting expenditure; it is not the fiscal surplus or a measure of total reserves. IRAS collections are already inside government operating revenue. IRAS’s 4 September 2026 release reports S$97.3 billion collected in FY2025/26, up 9.4%, representing 74.8% of government operating revenue at the release’s published precision. Adding that S$97.3 billion again would count much of the same revenue twice. NIRC includes up to 50% of expected long-term real returns on relevant net assets invested by GIC, MAS and Temasek, plus up to 50% of net investment income on remaining past reserves. Real means after inflation. Relevant net assets account for government liabilities. It is not simply half of this year’s combined accounting profit or dividends. This approach helps smooth spending across market cycles. A weak investment year does not mechanically cut the budget by the same amount. Persistent changes in asset values or expected long-term returns can still affect resources over time, so smoothing does not mean markets are irrelevant. Land-sale proceeds add to reserves rather than ordinary spendable operating revenue. The supplied revenue report was prepared in August 2026. Its statement that the latest IRAS series ends at FY2024/25 is now outdated. Its FY2026/27 total of approximately S$163.23 billion is derived using rounded components; MOF’s own published total is S$163.24 billion. Use the publisher’s aggregate at its stated precision and retain the rounding caveat. Keep FY2026/27 budget estimates separate from FY2025/26 audited actuals. The spending allowance from a long-term investment pool is not the same as the pool’s market gain in one year. Do not add IRAS to operating revenue, treat land-sale receipts as ordinary tax revenue, or add MAS, GIC and Temasek totals into a national-wealth figure. Internal claims and different measurement bases would need reconciliation. Use AGD for audited actuals, MOF for the current budget and NIRC rules, and IRAS for agency collections. Preserve fiscal-year labels and classification changes. budget-actual budget-estimate iras-2026 nirc reserves FY2025/26 audited values SGD Operating revenue 130,049,822,095.34 NIRC 27,522,875,864.50 Sum of the two revenue components 157,572,697,959.84 AGD Statement of Budget Outturn, physical PDF page 17 / printed page 9. Sum is calculated exactly from the displayed audited amounts; it is not the budget surplus. Audited actuals with separately labelled estimates

entries.title: How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit
entries.text: mas-accounts How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit Currency Currency translation is one part of the result; investment gains, liquidity-management costs and other expenses also matter. MAS holds foreign reserves for central-bank purposes while reporting its accounts in SGD. A foreign-currency asset can be unchanged in its own units yet translate into fewer SGD when SGD strengthens. That alone does not remove the foreign currency available for policy operations. The supplied FY2024/25 infographic is an accessible example: investment gains of S$31.4 billion, negative currency translation of S$3.4 billion and net money-market-operation and other costs of S$8.3 billion produce reported net profit of S$19.7 billion at the infographic’s displayed precision. It is a historical year, not the October 2026 result. The separately verified FY2025/26 MAS speech reports investment gains of S$39.8 billion, translation drag of S$16.4 billion, net money-market-operation and other costs of S$2.4 billion and a S$1.0 billion Consolidated Fund contribution. The reported net profit is S$20.0 billion. Showing only the S$16.4 billion drag would give an incomplete picture. The FY2021/22 statements provide the opposite historical example: an overall loss despite positive investment gains. That year’s main translation effects involved EUR, JPY and GBP. FY2025/26’s explanation principally involves USD and JPY. It would be inaccurate to describe all three years as simply USD losses. There are further measurement distinctions. MAS’s accounts have Group and Authority columns; its accounting investment result is not a fully comparable fund NAV total return. Liquidity operations incur interest costs and have policy objectives. A Consolidated Fund contribution, a later distribution of profit and NIRC are different fiscal concepts. For an individual who needs SGD to pay a mortgage or school fees, an FX translation reduction can be economically important. The fact that MAS can continue to conduct policy with its foreign assets does not imply a household should ignore its own currency mismatch. Read the whole income statement. A large deduction can coexist with a positive final result when other gains are larger. Headline amounts use issuer rounding. The FY2021/22 cost definition differs from later net-cost figures, so do not force those rounded components into a common exact waterfall. Net USD exposures and full hedges are not disclosed. Pair FX effects with the total result, state the affected currencies and period, and distinguish institutional policy capacity from personal SGD purchasing power. mas-2025-info mas-2025-accounts mas-2022-accounts mas-2022-info mas-2022-speech mas-2026 mas-fy2025-results mas-fy2022-highlights Financial year Investment gains Negative FX translation Reported net result 2021/22 S$4.0bn S$8.7bn −S$7.4bn 2024/25 S$31.4bn S$3.4bn +S$19.7bn 2025/26 update S$39.8bn S$16.4bn +S$20.0bn Published headline precision. Other costs and contributions affect the net result; these three columns alone are not a complete reconciliation. Historical uploaded evidence plus verified newer update
