entries.title: Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards
entries.text: gic-temasek Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards Singapore They have different jobs, portfolios and measurement systems; their headline results are not a league table. MAS is a central bank and needs liquid foreign reserves for monetary policy and financial stability. GIC manages government assets for long-term global purchasing power. Temasek is an investment company that owns its portfolio assets and reports shareholder returns. Their objectives, funding arrangements and investment flexibility differ. GIC’s uploaded FY2024/25 report explains its rolling twenty-year horizon. The separately verified FY2025/26 release reports 5.6% annualised nominal USD return and 3.4% annualised real return for the twenty years ended 31 March 2026. These are compounded annualised results over twenty years, not returns earned in just FY2025/26. A rolling figure can change because an old year drops out as well as because a new year enters. The historical GIC asset mix on page 14 is useful for explaining diversification. It is not a prescription for a client. GIC’s funding horizon and ability to hold private investments are different from a household’s. Its 2026 release also announces a Strategic Portfolio framework, so the older Reference Portfolio description should not be presented as the unqualified current framework. Temasek’s uploaded 2025 highlights reported S$434 billion net portfolio value, with a further S$35 billion uplift if the remaining unlisted investments were marked to market. The same-date comparable value was S$469 billion. The 2026 release reports S$518 billion after the full transition to mark-to-market reporting. The comparable increase is S$49 billion, not S$84 billion. Keep the bridge in sequence: S$434 billion plus S$35 billion equals S$469 billion at 31 March 2025; S$469 billion plus S$49 billion equals S$518 billion at 31 March 2026. The first step changes valuation basis at the same date. The second is the change between dates. Net portfolio value movements are not automatically identical to an investment return because capital flows and shareholder distributions can matter. Temasek’s 2026 one-year TSR was 10.5% in SGD, 12.9% at constant currency and 14.8% in USD. The arithmetic constant-currency gap is 2.4 percentage points. It reflects foreign-currency exposures collectively, not a disclosed USD-only loss. Headquarters, underlying business geography and currency exposure are also different classifications. Judge a hospital, an insurer and an investment fund against their own jobs. Comparing one headline number without its mandate and measurement would miss the purpose. Do not infer full government reserves, an undisclosed GIC asset base, or each entity’s NIRC allocation from these reports. Do not treat a valuation-method change as an investment gain. Compare like periods, like currencies and like valuation methods. Use institutions to learn process and discipline, then adapt to the client’s actual liabilities and liquidity needs. gic-2025 gic-2026 temasek-2025 temasek-2026 mas-2025-accounts nirc gic-fy2025-horizon gic-fy2025-allocation temasek-fy2025-overview Historical framework with current source corrections

entries.title: Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices
entries.text: temasek-bonds Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices Bonds The payment currency, coupon and discount curve can create very different prices even with the same guarantor. The issuer’s official register confirms the four bonds below. They are issued by Temasek Financial (I) Limited and guaranteed by Temasek Holdings (Private) Limited. Temasek explicitly states that its bonds are not guaranteed by the Singapore Government. The guarantee concerns contractual payments, not a stable market price or ready resale liquidity. A USD cash flow is valued against the USD interest-rate environment and relevant issuer spread. An SGD cash flow is valued against the SGD environment. A low fixed coupon becomes less competitive when the market requires a higher yield, so the price may fall well below face value. A higher-coupon bond can trade above face value and still offer a lower yield than its coupon. The supplied bilingual report uses two snapshot dates: 14 August 2026 for the 2039 examples, and 7 August 2026 for the 2070/2071 examples. These can illustrate the mechanism but must not appear as live dealing levels. The 2039 ask prices of 118.040 in SGD and 104.092 in USD are above par, not below par. Their location below an earlier chart high is a different claim. The report’s displayed yield-gap calculations are arithmetically consistent: 2.588% − 2.313% = 0.275 percentage point = 27.5 basis points, and 4.950% − 4.890% = 0.060 percentage point = 6 basis points. These are illustrative comparisons with particular government bonds. Maturity and cash-flow mismatches mean they are not precise option-adjusted or interpolated credit spreads. Pair each price with its own quote side. In the 2070 example, 5.475% is the bid yield paired with the 50.664 bid price, not the 51.076 ask price. The 2071 example likewise shows a 2.975% bid yield. An investor buying at an ask price needs the corresponding ask yield; this cannot be inferred by relabelling the bid yield. Compare total settlement cost and expected cash flows rather than the clean price alone. Clean price excludes accrued interest; the settlement amount normally includes it. Accrued interest paid to the seller should be reconciled with the next coupon in a dated cash-flow calculation. It should not be counted twice or mistaken for a permanent change to the coupon rate. If the starting clean price is already an executable ask, do not add the bid-ask spread again; add accrued interest and only separately charged fees or costs. A financed holding has additional moving parts: borrowing rates, loan currency, recognition ratios, collateral requirements and refinancing. These must use the actual facility terms. No advance ratio or margin-call threshold can be established from these public reports alone. The same company can issue two long-term payment promises in different currencies. Their values depend on what investors require for each currency and payment schedule. A low price alone is not proof of a bargain. High credit quality does not remove duration, FX, liquidity or leverage risks, and the Singapore Government does not guarantee these bonds. Obtain current executable bid/ask prices, settlement dates and terms. Compare yield, duration, spread, spending-currency exposure and ability to hold through volatility. temasek-bonds temasek-guarantee sgs treasury Bond currency and maturity Coupon Regulation S / local ISIN USD · 23 November 2039 5.3750% US87973RAB69 SGD · 7 December 2039 4.2000% SG7U77951360 USD · 6 October 2070 2.5000% US87973RAW07 SGD · 17 August 2071 2.8000% SGXF69044257 Official issue terms, checked 31 October 2026. entries.title: When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw
entries.text: alternatives-liquidity When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw Alternatives Private investments may earn returns while still limiting when, and at what price, you can recover your money. Alternatives is a broad label. Private equity owns companies; private credit lends to borrowers; real estate owns property; infrastructure owns or operates physical assets; hedge funds use varied trading strategies. Their risks are not interchangeable. The useful starting point is the economic source of return and the conditions for turning it back into cash. Private assets are often valued less frequently than exchange-traded securities. A smoother reported line may reflect the valuation process as well as the economics. It does not prove the asset would hold its value if sold immediately. Historical comparisons can also mix private-fund internal rates of return with public-market annual returns, making simple rankings misleading. JPMorgan’s page 58 shows a 4Q 2025 private-equity capital-call rate of 31% of beginning dry powder and a distribution rate of 14% of beginning NAV. These are preliminary rolling twelve-month rates with different denominators. Subtracting 14% from 31% would not calculate a valid net funding gap. A capital call asks an investor to deliver money already committed. A distribution returns cash. A fund can call capital before much cash comes back. An investor’s liquidity plan therefore needs to allow for commitment schedules and delays in exits, rather than assuming a stated annual return is spendable cash. Page 59 shows 2Q 2026 LP-led secondary pricing at 91% of NAV for buyout, 89% for credit, 79% for venture capital and 68% for real estate. These are market aggregates, not firm offers for a particular fund. A discount may reflect illiquidity, uncertainty or an out-of-date NAV; it is not automatically a bargain. Institutional portfolios can offer useful lessons about diversification and manager selection. Copying their allocation without matching their ability to meet future cash needs can create a very different risk. Liquidity is a portfolio property: even attractive long-term holdings can be unsuitable for money needed on a fixed near-term date. Owning a valuable apartment is different from having the sale proceeds in your bank account today. Timing and selling price both matter. Reported volatility, NAV, IRR, cash distributions and executable exit prices are different measures. Do not rank private products using a single yield or past-return figure. Before allocating, map capital commitments, redemption windows, gates, notice periods, valuation methods, fees and the cash reserve needed outside the investment. jpm-alternatives gic-2025 jpm-gta-p58 jpm-gta-p59 Lagged private-market observations with methodology

entries.title: Is all reported interest paid in cash
entries.text: private-credit Is all reported interest paid in cash Alternatives Some interest can be added to debt rather than received in cash, so reported income needs a cash-quality check. Payment in kind, or PIK, is a form of non-cash payment. In a loan context it often adds interest to the outstanding amount instead of paying it immediately. It can be a contractual feature rather than a default. It can also become more relevant when a borrower is conserving cash. JPMorgan page 69 shows PIK at 8.0% of interest and dividend income, on average for the Fitch-rated business development company sample, in 1Q 2026. This does not mean 8.0% of all private loans defaulted. It does not mean 8.0% of a particular fund’s assets are impaired. The population and denominator are essential to understanding the statistic. The same page compares public and private default trends with differing definitions and denominators. Private-credit defaults use counts of defaulted loans relative to loans; the public series uses issuer-based measures. Distressed exchanges also change the apparent default rate. A rewrite that strips away these differences can make a precise-looking chart misleading. For income-oriented clients, ask where the distribution comes from: cash interest, asset sales, borrowing, accumulated income or other sources permitted by the fund structure. A stated distribution rate is not necessarily a sustainable economic return. Asset-level yield and the investor’s net return can also diverge after fees, leverage and losses. The AI connection is worth monitoring, but it should be established issuer by issuer. Private financing can support productive investment; it can also concentrate financing risk in businesses whose revenues arrive later than their interest and capital spending. Aggregate charts identify questions for due diligence, not verdicts on every private-credit fund. Being told that someone owes you more is different from receiving more cash this month. Both may have value, but they fund your spending differently. PIK is not automatically default, and a lower reported default rate is not automatically evidence of a safer market if definitions differ. Review cash interest coverage, PIK share, non-accruals, amendments, leverage, covenants, recoveries and actual cash distributions at the specific fund or borrower level. jpm-alternatives jpm-gta-p69 1Q 2026 income-quality observation; not a default rate

entries.title: Build a portfolio that can survive the journey
entries.text: portfolio-actions Build a portfolio that can survive the journey Portfolio A sound long-term idea still needs enough liquidity and manageable concentration to survive difficult periods. JPMorgan’s drawdown chart covers full calendar years from 1980 to 2025. It reports an average intra-year decline of 14.2%, while 35 of the 46 years finished with positive price returns. The 2026 bar is year to date and is outside that full-year count. These are price returns, not returns including reinvested dividends. The lesson is about the route taken, not a guarantee of recovery. A good year can contain a frightening decline. A diversified index’s historical pattern does not imply that every individual share recovers, that every downturn is short, or that leverage is safe. Forced selling can make an interim loss permanent for the investor who must exit. Diversification should address sources of risk rather than product count. Inflation or interest-rate shocks can hurt stocks and long bonds together. AI-linked equities and AI-linked private lending can share a cash-flow driver. An offshore bond and a CHF loan introduce two currency exposures, and their movements should not be assumed to offset. For a reader deciding what to do, separate money by purpose before selecting products. Near-term spending requires dependable liquidity in the spending currency. Long-term growth capital can tolerate a different path. Income assets should be assessed for cash quality, while duration positions need a clear holding horizon and loss tolerance. Use rebalancing to maintain the chosen risk profile rather than allowing winners to determine it unintentionally. Review correlated exposures across direct holdings and funds. For borrowing, use the actual facility rules and stress asset prices, loan FX and financing rates together; the reports do not supply proprietary recognition rules or client-specific margin limits. The strategy implication is conditional: preserve the capacity to stay invested when the investment case remains sound, while retaining the flexibility to change course when evidence changes. This follows from the mechanics and historical evidence; it is not a recommendation to buy a particular security or copy an institution’s portfolio. A plan should fit the uncomfortable middle of the journey, not only the outcome you hope to reach at the end. Historical averages and previous recoveries are not a minimum future return or a deadline for the next recovery. Review cash needs, underlying concentration, duration, credit compensation, currency mismatch and funding resilience together. Record what evidence would change the investment case. jpm-markets jpm-alternatives mas-macro jpm-gtm-p16 Interpretation and practical monitoring

AMD led at +3.65%; Apple fell 1.90%. New in this review window: AMD reported Q3 results and Q4 guidance, while Meta filed final pricing for a $15 billion senior-note offering. Amazon filed a backward-looking 13F. Apple’s developer-preview item is explicitly earlier catch-up, not overnight breaking news. Review window: 4 November 2026, 04:00–08:00 SGT (3 November 20:00–4 November 00:00 UTC), with a 15-minute overlap. The previous 04:00 SGT edition and all older artifacts remain available unchanged. This edition replaces the prior in-progress session snapshots with the verified completed 3 November close and recomputed six-horizon returns. New research is separated from earlier catch-up; quiet names do not receive filler. News coverage is partial, not a complete newswire census. This is a dated personal research report, not a live portfolio, transaction record or signal to copy trades. No buy call or executed holding is implied. A thesis does not establish a purchase. No private notes or restricted research screenshots are included. Cumulative return = 100 × (3 November 2026 adjusted close ÷ baseline adjusted close − 1). The 1–6 calendar-month baselines are 2 October, 3 September, 3 August, 2 July, 3 June and 1 May 2026. October 3 and May 3 fall on weekends; July 3 is the observed US Independence Day market holiday, so preceding sessions are used. All 72 dated inputs were independently checked. Adjusted closes incorporate split and dividend/distribution adjustments; ordinary previous closes remain separate. These are cumulative returns before fees and taxes, not six individual monthly returns. We could not independently verify a reliably timestamped after-hours price for this edition. entries.title: Sharpe, Portfolios & Leverage | Wealth Research Add-on
entries.text: Sharpe, Portfolios & Leverage | Wealth Research Add-on ← Full wealth report Research library Sources Print / Save PDF PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17. Choose risk efficiency. Then choose the exposure. Why a higher-Sharpe portfolio may be a better starting point for leverage than the investment with the highest headline return. The investment decision has two parts: Choose a portfolio that uses risk efficiently. Then decide how much exposure the household can finance and withstand. Improving the portfolio and increasing its size are not the same decision. This new chapter extends Own the Assets. Understand the Borrowing. The original sections 1–16 and their visual companion remain available unchanged. Their Q2 2026 wealth figures remain anchored to the supplied FRED snapshot; this addition does not update those statistics or convert them into evidence of widespread high-Sharpe carry trading. Public research edition: this chapter uses original explanatory text, author calculations and newly drawn hypothetical examples. It reproduces no lecture screenshots, publisher charts or private account information. Illustrations are teaching assumptions, not actual investment records or forecasts. Question What the chapter establishes What should we own? Assess the combined portfolio, including how holdings move together. How much exposure should we take? Compare alternatives at the same risk or return target, then allow for actual financing. What can leverage accomplish? It can scale a worthwhile strategy. It does not manufacture investment skill or remove losses. What must remain feasible? Cash servicing, collateral headroom, currency exposure and repayment through stress. Return versus journey Read the ratio Diversification Equal-risk comparison Leverage algebra Real funding costs Bank illustration Efficient frontier Research evidence Currency and debt Limits and traps Measurement protocol Client framework Client-ready conclusion New sources Reading rule: “Research finding” refers to a cited publication. “Derivation” means algebra under stated conditions. “Hypothetical example” uses invented teaching inputs, visibly labelled and unrelated to any client portfolio. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.1 Same destination. A very different journey. Same endpoint, different ability to stay invested Original hypothetical diagram · index starts at 100 · six invented observations, no calendar period Two hypothetical paths from 100 to 120 Path A values: 100, 105, 102, 110, 113, 120. Path B: 100, 112, 78, 100, 105, 120. Values are invented to illustrate path risk, not investment performance. 70 80 90 100 110 120 Start Finish Path A Path B Author illustration. No Sharpe ratio or margin-call probability is inferred from these paths. Exact values behind the hypothetical paths Observation Path A Path B Start 100 100 1 105 112 2 102 78 3 110 100 4 113 105 Finish 120 120 A final return does not describe everything an investor experienced. The original diagram above uses two invented index paths that both finish at 120 from 100. A financing obligation can interrupt a journey even when the asset eventually recovers. An unleveraged owner may have the option to wait. A financed owner must also meet interest and collateral requirements along the way. An asset recovering later does not undo a sale required earlier to meet a loan obligation. [ 6 ] Look at the endpoint Also look at the path How much did the asset gain? How much did its market value fall before recovering? What income did it pay? Could that income and outside cash meet obligations when due? Was the eventual outcome attractive? Could the investor maintain the position without a forced exit? Interpretation: a steadier historical path may be helpful for a financed portfolio, but the picture alone cannot establish a Sharpe ratio, future loss distribution or margin-call probability. Equal ending wealth also does not imply equal arithmetic average returns. Client explanation: “We are not only choosing a destination. We are choosing a journey that your balance sheet can afford to complete.” PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.2 What the Sharpe ratio actually measures The Sharpe ratio measures average excess return per unit of variability in that excess return . It can describe historical experience or a forecast; the two must be labelled separately. [ 27 ] x t = R portfolio,t − r f,t S = mean(x t ) / standard deviation(x t ) The benchmark, currency, return frequency and sample period must match. The benchmark is not automatically the investor’s loan rate. Read the ratio as efficiency, not as an interest rate. A Sharpe ratio of 2 is not a 2% return and is not “twice as safe”. In the model it represents two units of excess return for each unit of volatility, measured consistently. No particular Sharpe number is a universal target or borrowing trigger. Use total returns. Coupon or distribution yield omits market-value changes. A yield-to-maturity quote divided by a price-volatility estimate is not a properly constructed historical Sharpe ratio. A price-only series and a distribution-inclusive series must not be mixed. Working principle: do not rank investments by return alone, but do not replace one simplistic ranking with an unquestioned Sharpe leaderboard. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.3 Improve the combination before increasing its size Individual Sharpe ratios do not tell us how well assets combine. Correlation is an additional input. A holding with a lower standalone Sharpe can improve a portfolio when its returns offset other exposures. [ 28 ] σ p 2 = w A 2 σ A 2 + w B 2 σ B 2 + 2w A w B ρσ A σ B Two-asset variance identity. The covariance term, not the number of line items, drives diversification. Diversification is about the relationship between returns: combining imperfectly correlated assets can improve risk-adjusted performance. Sharpe ratios themselves are not additive. Correlation changes the risk of a 50/50 mix Model portfolio volatility (%) · common zero-based scale Correlation +1.0 10.00% Correlation +0.5 8.66% Correlation 0 7.07% Correlation −0.5 5.00% 0 10 Invented inputs: each asset has 10% volatility, 8% expected return, and 50% weight. Risk-free rate 2%; correlations are assumptions, not estimates. No fees. Values rounded to two decimals. Hypothetical diversification arithmetic Correlation Expected return Volatility Sharpe +1.0 8% 10.00% 0.60 +0.5 8% 8.66% 0.69 0 8% 7.07% 0.85 −0.5 8% 5.00% 1.20 PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.4 Compare at the same risk, not just the same cash outlay The relevant question is not simply “Which line finishes highest?” Ask whether a more efficient portfolio can meet the desired return with less volatility, or deliver more expected excess return at an equal volatility budget. That comparison requires reliable forward-looking inputs and feasible scaling. [ 28 ] At a common volatility σ*: expected excess return = S × σ* At a common positive excess-return target m*: volatility = m* / S Idealised mean–variance derivation: a common risk-free rate, frictionless scaling and positive expected excess returns. Actual financing is addressed next. Hypothetical comparison: portfolio A has expected return 8%, volatility 10% and a 2% risk-free rate, giving S = 0.60. Portfolio B has expected return 10% and volatility 20% with the same benchmark, giving S = 0.40. Scaling A to twice its exposure gives 20% volatility and 14% expected return only in the frictionless model. These are invented annual model inputs, not forecasts. Central argument: a lower-return portfolio is not necessarily inferior. Its return per unit of risk may leave more room for sensible exposure sizing. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.5 Why leverage can scale a higher-Sharpe portfolio Define own equity E, borrowing D and gross assets A = E + D. Let λ = A / E be gross exposure per unit of equity. Here D is loan principal; Part I used L for that amount. A 1× exposure is unleveraged. λ is not a loan-to-value ratio. R equity = λR p − (λ − 1)r f μ equity − r f = λ(μ p − r f ) σ equity = λσ p S equity = λ(μ p − r f ) / (λσ p ) = S p Model conditions: positive constant exposure per measurement period; borrowing at the same constant risk-free rate; no incremental costs, FX mismatch, nonlinear payoffs or forced liquidation. For a single period, the equation is a balance-sheet identity before any external capital flows. Multi-period statistics require consistent rebalancing and return construction. [ 27 ] Unchanged Sharpe does not mean unchanged risk. In this ideal model, both expected excess return and volatility rise in proportion to λ. Leverage scales efficiency; it does not improve the underlying ratio. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.6 The real-world hurdle: borrowing costs and fees A loan normally has its own price. Retain the previous one-period, single-currency structure, but set the borrowing rate r b = r f + s. Let c be incremental fees divided by opening own equity, over the same period. Asset return μ p already includes any asset-level fees; do not subtract them twice. μ equity = λμ p − (λ − 1)(r f + s) − c = r f + λ(μ p − r f ) − (λ − 1)s − c If funding and fees are deterministic in this simplified calculation, σ equity = λσ p . Dividing the excess return by that volatility gives: S equity = S p − [(λ − 1)s + c] / (λσ p ) Author derivation. With a positive borrowing spread and positive fees, the financed Sharpe is below the underlying Sharpe in this model. Variable rates or FX require a richer risk model. When can the higher-Sharpe choice still win? Let A be the lower-volatility, higher-Sharpe portfolio and B an unleveraged comparison portfolio. Scale A to B’s volatility with λ = σ B / σ A > 1. Then: μ levered A − μ B = σ B (S A − S B ) − (λ − 1)s − c Potential advantage Must exceed σ B (S A − S B ) Extra financing spread and fees: (λ − 1)s + c A stronger underlying return/risk trade-off The implementation costs required to reach the common risk level Decision rule, not a recommendation: higher Sharpe creates a potential efficiency advantage. Actual funding terms determine how much survives. Equal volatility still does not mean equal tail loss, liquidity risk or margin risk. The derivation is symbolic. The separately labelled example below uses invented teaching inputs; no client return, current borrowing quote or suitable leverage amount is asserted. Compare expected return at the same 20% volatility Expected annual total return (%) · hypothetical inputs · not a performance record Portfolio B · unleveraged 10% Portfolio A · 2×, risk-free borrowing 14% Portfolio A · 2×, borrowing at 4% 12% 0 16 Same model assumptions as the text. The third bar includes a 2-percentage-point borrowing spread above the 2% risk-free rate, with no incremental fees. Equal volatility does not imply equal tail, liquidity or margin risk. Hypothetical exposure and funding comparison Case Gross exposure Borrowing rate Return Volatility Sharpe A unleveraged 1× None 8% 10% 0.60 B unleveraged 1× None 10% 20% 0.40 A scaled, ideal 2× 2% 14% 20% 0.60 A scaled, spread 2× 4% 12% 20% 0.50 PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.7 Connect the theory to the existing bank illustration Part I reproduces OCBC’s public hypothetical coupon example. It provides actual illustration inputs, but not the return series needed to calculate a Sharpe ratio . The website was rechecked for this addition. These are not current loan quotations or actual portfolio results. [ 7 ] Input or result Published / exact derived value Own capital E $750,000 Gross assets A $2,500,000 Loan D = A − E $1,750,000 Gross exposure λ = A / E 10 / 3 Debt / own equity = D / E 7 / 3 Loan-to-value D / A 70% Coupon cash $125,000 Interest at 2.50% $43,750 Net coupon at 2.50% $81,250 Interest at 4.50% $78,750 Net coupon at 4.50% $46,250 Exact financing sensitivity: increasing the loan rate from 2.50% to 4.50% reduces annual net coupon by $35,000. Relative to own equity, that reduction is: $35,000 / $750,000 = 7 / 150 = 14 / 3 percentage points The fraction is left exact rather than rounded. This is the reduction in cash return on own capital, not a calculated Sharpe ratio. The published example uses an unnamed $ currency. Risk interpretation: for the same underlying portfolio and the ideal fixed-rate model, exposure of 10 / 3 scales its volatility by 10 / 3. The original maximum-capacity example also has zero initial lending headroom: 70% × $2,500,000 − $1,750,000 = $0 Important boundary: higher coupon cash does not establish a higher Sharpe ratio. Even a genuinely high-Sharpe portfolio should not be assumed safe at maximum lending capacity. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.8 Choose the portfolio. Then set the risk budget. Separate portfolio construction from exposure sizing. First, select a mix offering an attractive expected return for its volatility. Second, select the amount of exposure. Adding cash reduces risky exposure; borrowing increases it. Choosing a more volatile asset is not the only route to seeking a higher return. [ 30 ] The highest-Sharpe tangent-portfolio rule depends on its assumptions: a suitable mean–variance objective, a common risk-free rate, reliable expected returns and covariances, and feasible borrowing or lending. With costly or restricted borrowing, the attainable set changes. Household liabilities and non-volatility risks also matter. Recent research qualifies the simple rule. Moshe Levy’s 2026 study finds that realistic borrowing restrictions can substantially weaken the alignment between Sharpe rankings and investor welfare; it examines geometric-mean-based alternatives. This does not make Sharpe useless. It means the best feasible choice need not be the highest standalone Sharpe. [ 34 ] Use this workflow: construct → compare → size → finance → stress-test. Do not treat the tangent point as permission for unlimited borrowing. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.9 Research supports the principle, not a guaranteed outcome Leverage aversion: riskier assets are not automatically better Betting Against Beta studies leverage constraints and evidence across multiple markets. Its low-beta / high-beta strategy is not simply “buy any safe asset with debt”. It combines leveraged low-beta holdings with a short high-beta leg and finds vulnerability when funding constraints tighten. The relevance is that return-seeking demand can favour intrinsically risky assets, leaving opportunities in how risk is packaged. [ 29 ] Risk parity: balance risk before scaling it Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity considers allocations that spread risk more evenly and then scale exposure. Its evidence supports studying portfolio risk contributions rather than dollar weights alone. A bond-heavy allocation, however, is not automatically the highest-Sharpe mix, and risk parity is not synonymous with Sharpe maximisation. [ 30 ] Buffett: quality selection and funding structure together The published 2018 Buffett’s Alpha study reports a Berkshire Sharpe ratio of 0.79 and estimated average leverage of about 1.7 to 1 . Its interpretation links results to cheap, lower-risk, high-quality equities and leverage. Those are sample estimates, not a current allocation or a leverage recommendation. [ 31 ] Version discipline: AQR’s accompanying web summary quotes 0.76 and about 1.6 to 1, reflecting a different presentation of the research. This chapter uses the published article’s 0.79 and about 1.7 to 1, without mixing them with the earlier figures. [ 31 , 35 ] Funding is part of the strategy. The authors discuss low-cost insurance-float financing in their summary. A private investor’s callable portfolio loan is not equivalent to that corporate funding structure. Copying exposure without matching the resilience of funding would miss a central implementation difference. [ 6 , 35 ] The stronger lesson: select worthwhile assets and an effective combination, then use financing that permits the strategy to survive. The objective is not to copy somebody else’s leverage number. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.10 Measure the financed position, not just the bond or fund Three things must remain distinct: the asset’s standalone Sharpe; the financed investor-equity Sharpe; and lending headroom. The first can be attractive while the second is damaged by funding or FX, and the third can fail before a long-term thesis is realised. [ 6 , 27 ] CHF debt changes the USD investment’s return distribution For one period with unchanged principal and interest accruing to the end, let q be USD per CHF and i CHF the contractual period interest rate. The effective USD return-cost of the debt is: R D = (1 + i CHF ) × (q 1 / q 0 ) − 1 R E = λR A − (λ − 1)R D − c Author balance-sheet derivation. R_A is the USD asset total return. Costs c are measured against opening equity. Interim interest payments require their actual dates and exchange rates. Before additional random fees and capital flows, the corresponding variance identity is: Var(R E ) = λ²Var(R A ) + (λ − 1)²Var(R D ) − 2λ(λ − 1)Cov(R A , R D ) A negative covariance is dangerous here: the USD assets can fall while the USD repayment cost of CHF debt rises. A Sharpe ratio calculated from the USD bond alone misses that interaction. For an SGD-based comparison, translate the complete net position and cash flows into SGD and use a matching benchmark. A bond coupon is not a stable price Bond total returns incorporate market values, accrued interest and distributions. Maturity and issuer obligations matter, but the ability to hold until maturity is a separate constraint when collateral is marked along the way. A high advance ratio does not certify a high Sharpe. [ 6 , 21 ] Accounting control: use net investor equity after liabilities. If NAV is already net of the CHF loan, do not subtract that loan a second time. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.11 Do not mistake a smooth line for a safe investment Sharpe can miss or obscure Required additional check Rare, severe losses Drawdown, downside scenarios and loss concentration Illiquid or smoothed prices Reliable executable valuations and liquidation time Changing correlations Joint stress across the whole portfolio Funding and margin constraints Haircuts, loan terms and outside liquidity Short samples or selected backtests Out-of-sample results, robustness and estimation uncertainty Research warning: Getmansky, Lo and Makarov show how illiquidity and smoothed returns can distort measured risk and motivate smoothing-adjusted Sharpe estimates. A steady reported NAV is not sufficient evidence of a steady economic value. [ 33 ] Product boundary: a cap/floor payoff, an insurance illustration or a sequence of declared crediting rates cannot be assigned a superior investable Sharpe without comparable economic returns, fees, surrender terms, liquidity and liabilities. This chapter does not calculate a product-specific or client-portfolio Sharpe ratio. No universal threshold: a Sharpe of 2 or any other single threshold should not become an automatic borrowing trigger. A high historical number is a prompt for verification, not permission to increase debt. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.12 Calculate it consistently, then test its reliability A valid comparison needs comparable inputs. Use aligned total-return observations, one reporting currency, a matched benchmark and clearly defined fees. Distinguish an actual investor-equity series from a fixed-weight backtest. Do not reconstruct investment returns by tracing a picture. Historical period Sharpe = mean(x t ) / s x Under the usual independent-observation test: t = S period √n If simple annualisation is valid: S annual = S period √k Therefore: t = S annual √(n / k) n = number of observations; k = observations per year. Testing the mean excess return is not the same as testing raw return against zero unless the benchmark is zero. An exact classical t-test additionally assumes independent, identically distributed normal observations; large-sample approximations require suitable regularity conditions. Andrew Lo’s research matters here: Sharpe estimates have sampling uncertainty, and serial correlation can invalidate routine square-root annualisation. A smooth-looking series can therefore produce misleading confidence and rankings. [ 32 ] Reporting standard: show period, frequency, currency, benchmark, gross/net basis, observation count and valuation source beside every ratio. Show drawdown and margin stress separately. Use “not calculable from available data” where a required input is absent. Use arithmetic excess-return observations for the ratio. Report compounded growth separately; do not silently substitute CAGR into the standard Sharpe numerator. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.13 Turn the idea into a portfolio-financing decision The objective is a better feasible portfolio, not the largest obtainable loan. The following is a proposed decision framework, not a client allocation or a prescribed leverage ratio. Step Evidence required Decision implication 1. Establish the base portfolio Holdings, weights, market values, total-return history and liabilities Do not use financing to make an unsuitable asset appear attractive. 2. Compare combinations Return, volatility and covariance on the same basis A diversifying holding can be useful even with a lower standalone Sharpe. 3. Choose a risk budget Loss capacity, cash needs, horizon and downside scenarios Equal volatility is a comparison device, not a complete definition of equal risk. 4. Price financing Actual rate, spread, fees, FX and hedge terms Test whether the efficiency advantage survives the extra costs. 5. Test path survival Stressed collateral, lower advance ratios, adverse FX and renewal terms Keep repayment resources that do not depend on the same assets recovering. 6. Monitor and rebalance Net equity, cash servicing, debt and headroom Use actual results, not unchanged historical Sharpe, to reassess exposure. UBS’s Singapore Lombard guidance explicitly identifies diversification, unused lending capacity and additional liquid assets as risk-mitigation measures. Those controls address funding resilience; they do not convert a volatile portfolio into a guaranteed outcome. [ 6 ] Recommended dashboard separation Investment efficiency: total return, excess return, volatility, portfolio Sharpe and correlation assumptions. Loss capacity: drawdown, concentrated exposures and stress losses. Financing: actual interest, debt principal, loan currency and reset dates. Survival: lending value, utilisation, collateral shortfall and independent liquidity. Go / no-go principle: proceed only when the asset mix, after-cost economics and funding resilience work together. An unleveraged portfolio remains a complete and legitimate choice. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.14 The message to retain The argument is stronger than “wealthy people borrow”. Asset ownership creates participation in financial returns. Diversification can improve how efficiently the portfolio uses risk. Suitable financing may then adjust the scale of that exposure without forcing the investor to choose intrinsically riskier assets. The benefit must still survive costs and real constraints. [ 29 , 30 ] Plain-language explanation “We should not automatically choose the investment with the highest advertised return. We should first examine how much risk is required to pursue that return, and how the investments behave together. A well-constructed portfolio with a stronger return-to-risk profile may be a better foundation. Where suitable, financing can increase exposure to that portfolio rather than pushing us towards a much riskier asset just to seek a higher number. Borrowing still increases the amount we can lose, and its cost and repayment conditions matter. We therefore assess the portfolio, the loan and the ability to remain invested as one complete plan. The aim is not maximum return at any cost. It is an appropriate return from a portfolio and financing structure that we can sustain.” Own the assets. Improve the mix. Size the exposure. Protect the ability to hold. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE New research and source links New research and source checks for the Sharpe chapter, accessed 4 November 2026. Hyperlinked titles lead to the underlying material; some full articles require publisher access. The original 25-source list remains in Part I, section 16 . Numbering here follows the expanded research edition; reference 26 is not used in this public chapter. [27] William F. Sharpe. The Sharpe Ratio (1994) Author-hosted article. Excess-return definition, scale independence and limitations. [28] William F. Sharpe. Morningstar’s Performance Measures: Sharpe Ratios Author-hosted explanation of equal-risk comparisons, borrowing/lending and portfolio correlation. [29] Andrea Frazzini and Lasse Heje Pedersen. Betting Against Beta (2014) Journal of Financial Economics 111, 1–25. Author-hosted full paper; leverage constraints and funding risk. [30] Cliff Asness, Andrea Frazzini and Lasse Heje Pedersen. Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity (2012) Author-firm research summary. Risk allocation followed by exposure scaling; not a universal risk-parity endorsement. [31] Andrea Frazzini, David Kabiller and Lasse Heje Pedersen. Buffett’s Alpha (2018) Financial Analysts Journal 74(4), 35–55. Published abstract: Sharpe 0.79; estimated average leverage about 1.7 to 1. [32] Andrew W. Lo. The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios (2002) Financial Analysts Journal 58(4), 36–52. Sampling uncertainty, serial correlation and annualisation. [33] Mila Getmansky, Andrew W. Lo and Igor Makarov.
